overview: COVID-19 (Coronavirus Disease 2019) is a contagious respiratory illness caused by SARS-CoV-2. It affects multiple organ systems with a clinical spectrum ranging from asymptomatic infection to severe disease and death. First identified in Wuhan, China in late 2019, it became a global pandemic in 2020.

types.name: Mild COVID-19
types.description: Symptoms like fever, cough, and fatigue without shortness of breath or pneumonia. Managed at home with rest and monitoring.

types.name: Moderate COVID-19
types.description: Lower respiratory tract involvement with SpO2 90–94%. May require supplemental oxygen but not ICU care.

types.name: Severe COVID-19
types.description: SpO2 below 90%, severe pneumonia, or signs of organ stress. Requires hospitalization and high-flow oxygen or ventilation.

types.name: Critical COVID-19
types.description: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), septic shock, or multi-organ failure. Requires ICU admission.

types.name: Long COVID (Post-COVID Condition)
types.description: Persistent symptoms lasting beyond 4–12 weeks after initial infection including fatigue, brain fog, and breathlessness.

symptoms: Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
causes: Inhalation of respiratory droplets or aerosols from infected persons
Touching contaminated surfaces and then touching face (less common)
Close contact in poorly ventilated indoor spaces
Exposure in healthcare settings without proper PPE
diagnosis: RT-PCR (reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction) — gold standard
Rapid Antigen Test (RAT) — quick results, lower sensitivity
CT scan of chest — shows ground-glass opacities in pneumonia
Blood tests: CBC, CRP, D-dimer, ferritin, LFT, RFT
Antibody/serology test — detects past infection, not suitable for acute diagnosis

antiviral_drugs: Remdesivir — for hospitalized patients requiring oxygen
Nirmatrelvir + Ritonavir (Paxlovid) — for high-risk outpatients within 5 days of symptoms
Molnupiravir — alternative antiviral for eligible outpatients
anti_inflammatory: Dexamethasone — for patients requiring supplemental oxygen or ventilation
Baricitinib or Tocilizumab — for hospitalized patients with severe inflammation
supportive_care: Oxygen therapy via nasal cannula, face mask, or high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO)
home_management: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and pain
Monitor SpO2 with pulse oximeter daily
Isolate to prevent spread to others
Seek help immediately if SpO2 drops below 94%

complications: Viral pneumonia and ARDS (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome)
Blood clots (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism)
Neurological effects — stroke, encephalitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome
Long COVID — persistent fatigue, cognitive impairment, breathlessness
prevention: Vaccination with approved COVID-19 vaccines (primary series + boosters)
Wear well-fitted mask (N95/KN95) in crowded or poorly ventilated spaces
Wash hands regularly with soap for at least 20 seconds
Maintain physical distance from sick individuals
Ensure good ventilation indoors — open windows or use air purifiers
Avoid large gatherings during high transmission periods
Stay home and isolate if symptomatic
emergency_signs: Severe shortness of breath at rest or inability to speak in full sentences
High fever (above 39.4°C / 103°F) not responding to medication

faqs.question: How long should I isolate if I test positive for COVID-19?
faqs.answer: Generally, isolate for at least 5 days from symptom onset. You may end isolation after day 5 if fever-free for 24 hours without fever-reducing medicine and symptoms are improving. Wear a mask around others through day 10.

faqs.question: Can I get COVID-19 again after recovering?
faqs.answer: Yes. Reinfection is possible, especially with new variants. Immunity from prior infection wanes over months. Vaccination — even after natural infection — significantly reduces risk and severity of reinfection.

faqs.question: What is Long COVID?
faqs.answer: Long COVID (Post-COVID Condition) is defined by WHO as symptoms persisting 3 months after COVID-19 infection, lasting at least 2 months. Common symptoms include fatigue, brain fog, breathlessness, and joint pain. Vaccinated individuals are less likely to develop Long COVID.

faqs.question: Do antibiotics work for COVID-19?
faqs.answer: No. COVID-19 is caused by a virus, and antibiotics are ineffective against viruses. Antibiotics may be prescribed only if a secondary bacterial infection is confirmed.
